record_type_quote: In light of new, improved standards for evidentiary value, we conducted high-powered registered replications of the central paradigms used in prosocial spending research.

targets.authors: Aknin, L. B., Barrington-Leigh, C. P., Dunn, E. W., Helliwell, J. F., Burns, J., Biswas-Diener, R., . . . Norton, M. I.
targets.title: Prosocial spending and well-being: Cross-cultural evidence for a psychological universal.
targets.evidence_quote: The first experiment investigated the immediate emotional rewards of prosocial (vs. personal) spending by providing participants the opportunity to spend a small monetary windfall on edible treats for themselves or an unknown sick child at a local children’s hospital (see Aknin et al., 2013, Study 3). Afterward, participants reported their current well-being. The second experiment used a recollection procedure (as in Aknin et al., 2013, Studies 2a-b) in which participants were randomly assigned to reflect upon a previous purchase made for themselves or others before reporting their well-being.
targets.outcome_quote: Taken together, these studies support the hypothesis that spending money on others does promote happiness, but demonstrate that the magnitude of the effect depends on several methodological features.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors give an overall positive verdict across the three studies, so rule 1 determines successful. Experiment 2 failed and Experiments 1 and 3 supported the prediction; the explicit whole-project conclusion outweighs those differing individual results. Smaller effects do not alone imply mixed.

reasoning: Verified title, all five authors and published DOI in the accepted manuscript. All three experiments re-test paradigms explicitly attributed to Aknin et al. (2013), one original paper. Dunn et al. (2008) is an earlier foundational study, not the specific immediate target; Dunn et al. (2014) is background. Other cited replications and review-table papers were not re-tested individually.
